posts.title: Keeping an idea secret before you file
posts.excerpt: Why the months before filing matter, and what counts as telling the world.
posts.content:
In most countries a patent can only be granted for something that is new. Anything you have made public before the filing date can count against you, including things you said yourself.

What counts as public

A talk at a meet-up, a post with a photo, a pitch deck sent without a confidentiality agreement, a crowdfunding page, a product on sale. Showing a prototype to a friend in your workshop is usually fine, but it is better to ask first.

What you can do

Share details only under a written confidentiality agreement, and keep a short note of who saw what and when. If you have already said something in public, tell us at the first conversation. It may limit your options, but it does not always end them.

Once the application is filed, the filing date is fixed and you are free to talk. That is why we sometimes file a simple first application early, and improve the detail afterwards.

posts.title: What a patent search tells you, and what it does not
posts.excerpt: How to read the result of a patentability search without over-reading it.
posts.content:
A patentability search looks through patent databases and other published sources for things close to your idea. It is done before drafting so that the claims can be shaped around what already exists.

What you get

A written opinion that lists the closest documents, says how they differ from your idea, and gives our view on whether a claim is likely to be new and inventive. The fee is fixed.

What it cannot tell you

No search is complete. Some applications are not published for eighteen months, and some documents are hard to find in any language. A good result is encouraging, not a promise, and a poor result is useful too: it can save you the cost of an application that would not succeed.

We explain the result in a short call. Many inventors decide on the spot to change the design, and often that is the best money they spend.

posts.title: How claims work, in plain words
posts.excerpt: The claims, not the drawings, decide what a patent protects.
posts.content:
A patent application has a description and drawings, but the part that matters most is the list of claims at the end. Each claim defines, in one long sentence, what you can stop others from doing.

A broad claim and narrower ones

The first claim is usually the broadest. It lists only the features that are really necessary. The claims that follow add detail, so that if the broad claim is refused after examination, there is something narrower to fall back on.

Why wording matters

A claim that is too narrow is easy to design around. A claim that is too broad may be refused because it covers something that already exists. Drafting is the work of finding the space between them, and we do it with you at the table.

Our fixed fee for an application covers up to fifteen claims. If your invention needs more, we say so before we start.

posts.title: Trademark classes explained
posts.excerpt: Why a name is registered for goods and services, not in general.
posts.content:
A trademark is registered for particular goods and services, grouped into 45 classes. Clothing is in one class, software in another, advertising services in a third.

Choosing the classes

You need a class for each kind of thing you sell now, and for what you are likely to sell soon. Too few leaves a gap, and too many costs money and invites objections. Our application fee covers one class, and each further class costs less.

Why a search comes first

A name may be free in one class and taken in another. Our clearance search looks at identical and similar marks in the classes you need, in the countries where you will trade. It is a guide to risk, not a guarantee. After it, we agree the name and the classes before anything is filed.

posts.title: What an examination report looks like
posts.excerpt: A first report is normal. Here is what it contains and how we answer.
posts.content:
A few months or a few years after filing, the patent office writes back. This is an examination report, and receiving one is entirely normal. Most applications receive at least one.

What is inside

The examiner lists documents they consider close to your invention and says which claims they consider unclear, not new, or obvious. There is a time limit to reply, and our records team writes it into the diary on the day the report arrives.

How we answer

We read the documents with you, then reply with arguments, amended claims or both. Sometimes a short call with the examiner settles a point faster than another letter. Each reply to a report has a fixed fee. The office decides at the end, and neither we nor anyone else can promise the outcome.

posts.title: PCT timing, in plain words
posts.excerpt: How the twelve-month window and the WIPO route fit together.
posts.content:
A first application gives you priority for twelve months. During that year you can file the same invention in other countries and treat the first filing date as your starting point.

What the PCT does

The Patent Cooperation Treaty, run by WIPO, lets you file a single international application. It does not give you a worldwide patent. It gives you more time, typically up to thirty months from the first filing, to decide which countries you want, and a search report to inform that choice.

The cost question

The big costs arrive when you enter each country: official fees and translations. We quote translations in writing before they start, and we will tell you if a country is not worth the money.

Put the twelve-month date in your diary. We also write it in ours, twice.
